content_text:
Israeli forces' operations, settler violence, demolitions and movement restrictions continued to drive displacement and undermine Palestinian livelihoods and access to essential services across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. In herding and farming communities, particularly in Masafer Yatta and the Jordan Valley, the combined impact of violence, access restrictions and the destruction of essential infrastructure is increasingly undermining communities' ability to remain on their land.

During the reporting period, an Israeli settlement guard shot and killed a Palestinian man near Dura al Qar' (Ramallah). According to the Israeli military, a settlement security coordinator opened fire when two Palestinian men approached Beit El settlement, killing one, while the other was arrested. The Israeli military stated that the incident was under investigation.

Overall, 47 Palestinians, including six children, were injured during the reporting period, of whom eight were injured by Israeli settlers and 39 by Israeli forces. Twelve Palestinians (26 per cent) were injured in the context of settler attacks, including three in incidents related to the olive harvest. Operations by Israeli forces displaced 11 Palestinians, while demolitions displaced another 67.

The cumulative impact of violence, demolitions, displacement and movement restrictions is also taking a toll on Palestinians' mental health and psychosocial well-being. According to a report published by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) on 19 November, exposure to violence accounted for approximately 70 per cent of recorded reasons for seeking mental health care from MSF teams in the West Bank between October 2022 and April 2026. The report also found that anxiety and depression-related symptoms accounted for about two thirds of reported mental health conditions. These needs are compounded by restrictions on access to health services and humanitarian assistance.

Since the beginning of October, intensified movement restrictions imposed by the Israeli authorities, alongside recurrent settler attacks, have increasingly undermined access to essential services, livelihoods and humanitarian assistance in Masafer Yatta, in southern Hebron governorate. Restrictions on vehicle access to the area designated by the Israeli authorities as "Firing Zone 918" have severely disrupted deliveries of food, water and animal fodder, as well as access to health and education services. These arrangements are insufficient to accommodate daily schooling, emergency medical needs and regular deliveries of essential supplies, including water.

According to the Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) Cluster, water trucking operations serving more than 1,500 Palestinians across 10 of the 12 remaining communities within the Israeli-designated firing zone in Masafer Yatta remain severely constrained. The programme was initiated in late April following settler attacks in January and February 2026 that severed the communities' water supply network, which partners remain unable to restore. The programme was recently expanded to cover three additional communities outside the firing zone. Following limited deliveries in November, Israeli settlers reportedly seized a water truck and physically assaulted its driver on 14 November near Isfai al Fouqa. Although residents and the village council subsequently retrieved the truck, deliveries were further disrupted. So far in November, limited quantities of water have reached only three communities inside the firing zone and two outside it.

Between 1 October and 23 November, Israeli forces confiscated at least 18 Palestinian-owned vehicles, including agricultural tractors, private vehicles and a vehicle belonging to a local organization. According to the village council, Israeli authorities had verbally communicated through the Palestinian District Coordination and Liaison Office that vehicles operating within the designated area, except those belonging to the Palestinian Ministry of Education, would be subject to confiscation. The closure of a road gate near Carmel settlement on 23 October has further restricted movement along key routes serving at least 5,800 Palestinians south of Yatta. The restrictions also coincide with the lambing season, a critical period for herding communities, with disruptions to fodder supplies threatening livestock health and productivity and the sustainability of household livelihoods.

The area was designated by the Israeli authorities as a firing zone in the 1980s. On 17 June 2025, the Israeli military issued a notice that the area would be used for military training. In conjunction with this announcement, the Israeli Civil Administration issued a planning directive allowing the retroactive dismissal of Palestinian planning applications, further heightening the risk of mass demolitions and displacement. Since 2009, Israeli authorities have demolished 422 Palestinian-owned structures in the firing zone area of Masafer Yatta, including 240 (57 per cent) that had been provided as humanitarian assistance. Nearly a quarter of these structures (97) were demolished in 2026 alone, displacing 118 Palestinians, including 58 children, and otherwise affecting 136 people. Agricultural, livelihood and water and sanitation structures accounted for approximately 60 per cent of all structures demolished this year. Schools, health clinics and other essential civilian infrastructure remain at risk of demolition.

Since January 2023, more than 160 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage have been documented in communities in Masafer Yatta located within the Israeli-designated firing zone, including 41 so far in 2026. Attacks have repeatedly targeted homes, water and electricity infrastructure, livestock, agricultural assets and vehicles used to transport essential supplies and students. In some cases, settlers have subsequently attacked homes belonging to families already displaced, further undermining prospects for return. Since the beginning of 2026, 50 Palestinians, including 29 children, have been displaced due to settler violence and related access restrictions. The combined impact of recurrent demolitions, sustained settler violence, intensified movement restrictions and the erosion of livelihoods is heightening the risk of further displacement.

Protection partners continue to provide legal assistance, including follow-up on vehicle confiscations and access restrictions, alongside psychosocial support, specialized child protection services, gender-based violence prevention and mitigation interventions, cash for protection and protective presence where access allows. Given restrictions on vehicle access, partners are also supporting community-based protection initiatives to identify urgent needs and facilitate referrals, documenting incidents and their humanitarian impact, and raising urgent protection concerns through existing coordination mechanisms.

During the reporting period, Israeli authorities demolished or forced Palestinians to demolish 79 Palestinian-owned structures across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, for lacking Israeli-issued building permits, displacing 67 Palestinians, including 29 children, and otherwise affecting more than 3,000 people. Of the demolished structures: 69 were in Area C, nine in East Jerusalem and one in Area B, while 13 structures had been provided as humanitarian assistance. Agricultural, water and sanitation structures accounted for more than half of all structures demolished, illustrating the wider impact of demolitions on livelihoods and access to essential services.

In the northern Jordan Valley, on 22 November, Israeli authorities demolished all 44 remaining structures in Khirbet Samra (Tubas), leaving the community's last two resident households, comprising 19 people, including seven children, without shelter. The demolitions also affected essential infrastructure and livelihood assets, including animal shelters, fodder storage facilities, water tanks, latrines provided as humanitarian assistance and solar power systems. At least 15 of the structures belonged to two households comprising eight people who had been displaced to Tubas city in March 2026 following recurrent settler attacks and harassment. According to affected families, they received no recent demolition orders or advance warning, preventing them from salvaging their properties and essential assets. The destruction of all remaining structures further undermines prospects for previously displaced families to return.

The Jordan Valley accounts for nearly one third of all displacement due to settler violence, related access restrictions and demolitions for lacking Israeli-issued building permits across the West Bank so far in 2026 (1,567 out of 4,992). Within the Jordan Valley, settler violence and related access restrictions accounted for 87 per cent of such displacement.

Elsewhere in the northern Jordan Valley, demolitions in Ein al Beida and Bardala (Tubas) displaced three Palestinians and otherwise affected 37 people, including 18 children. The destruction of greenhouses, crops, irrigation infrastructure, agricultural storage facilities and roadside shops further undermined affected families' livelihoods.

In Area B, on 18 November, Israeli authorities damaged and confiscated pumping equipment and associated infrastructure at a groundwater well in Bidya (Salfit), citing the lack of Israeli-issued permits and rendering the well inoperable. The well served at least 3,000 Palestinians and supplied a significant proportion of the municipality's water for domestic and agricultural purposes. According to the WASH Cluster, the loss of this water source has exacerbated water shortages and increased reliance on costly water trucking, with estimated losses exceeding NIS 600,000 (US$177,537).

In East Jerusalem, demolitions in Jabal al Mukabbir, Al Bustan in Silwan and the Ein Jweizeh area of Al Walaja displaced four households comprising 16 people, including six children. Three quarters of those displaced were forced to demolish their own homes to avoid additional fines and demolition costs.

Displacement in the context of Israeli forces' operations also continued. On 23 November, Israeli forces forcibly displaced three Palestinian households comprising 11 people from a residential building in Al Hadaf neighbourhood of Jenin city, citing its location within the area of the ongoing Israeli forces' operation in Jenin refugee camp. According to an affected resident, the families were given approximately only 10 minutes to vacate their homes. They are temporarily staying with relatives.

During the reporting period, 55 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage were documented across 46 Palestinian communities, compared with a weekly average of 53 such attacks so far in 2026. Attacks continued to target residential property, livelihood assets and essential infrastructure, further undermining living conditions in affected communities.

On 17 and 19 November, Israeli settlers reportedly seized a water tank in Khirbet al Marajem, near Duma (Nablus), and vandalized a main water pipeline in Al Mas'udiya (Nablus), disrupting water supply to approximately 80 people in the latter community. Residents there have also reportedly been without electricity for more than two months after settlers damaged electricity infrastructure and prevented repairs. Other incidents involved the burning of Palestinian-owned vehicles in Hebron governorate and the theft of an electricity generator and destruction of an agricultural structure in Deir Ballut (Salfit).

title: UN sacked Palestinian staff on back of unproven Israeli allegations, tribunal rules
summary_or_snippet: Judgment casts doubt on evidence linking aid workers to Hamas and says humanitarian efforts in Gaza were damaged A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based "almost entirely" on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza. The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

title: Palestinian journalist killed by Israel in Gaza wins Rory Peck prize
summary_or_snippet: Mariam Dagga shares award with two of her colleagues from AP for 'powerful coverage' of human cost of war Mariam Dagga, the Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in Gaza in an Israeli strike, has posthumously won the prestigious Rory Peck prize for freelance video journalists, the organisers announced on Wednesday. She shares the award with two of her colleagues from the Associated Press (AP), Abdel Kareem Hana and Jehad Alshrafi, "for their powerful coverage of the human cost of the war" in the Palestinian territory, the Rory Peck Trust said.

title: Pro-Palestine activist sought by US in extradition case: 'I still have a right to my beliefs'
summary_or_snippet: James 'Fergie' Chambers, at center of legal fight, says he 'should not be unjustly accused' because of leftwing views James "Fergie" Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor controversially sought in extradition by the US, has told the Guardian that he is "not asking anyone to endorse my ideas or not think I'm a jerk - but I still have a right to my beliefs and should not be unjustly accused because of them". Chambers's case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.
